title: Tryst with libraries
author: Murali  M. Mallareddy
content_html:
Libraries have always occupied a special place in my life, as reading was my forte from a young age. In our village, we had a very small branch library with fewer books than the personal collection of an average avid reader, all stacked precariously on the damp floor without a single rack to hold them. The library used to function depending on the mood of an alcoholic librarian who used to stay near our home. A handful of students and job seekers were regulars for reading newspapers and magazines.

I got hooked to pulp fiction and read most of the vernacular literature, as reading novels was taboo for students in those days. One day, the librarian threatened me with a warning to focus on studies; else, he would complain about my reading affair to my mother.

I switched to Plan B and convinced my mother for a nominal subscription which allowed to take home weekly one book in her name. At home, I was to be doubly cautious lest my mom discover my reading, which she did one day and subjected me to severe punishment.

Later during my intermediate days in the neighbouring town, I use to skip classes and spend time in tiny dark rooms and verandahs functioning as libraries. There I developed a nasty habit of tearing pages of serialised novels off weekly magazines, only to make a bound copy of them as personal collection. One day, the librarian laid a trap and caught my misdeed red-handed. He confiscated my wristwatch as security until I pay a penalty. Next day I paid 50 rupees and got back my watch. Later, at home, my mother was searching for a missing 50-rupee note for the next two days.

After joining the Air Force, wherever I was posted to, I made good use of well maintained state-of-the-art libraries at our units. Whenever I reported to a new unit, I used to search for the nearest library and post office and usually had a good rapport with librarians and postmen. I use to spend most of my off-duty time in libraries. At times, whenever the exercise of disposing of old and damaged books used to take place, I was the one to acquire those old and smelly books with damaged spines and tinted pages with much awe as an invaluable possession for a throwaway price.

During my tenure in Lucknow, my senior colleague and mentor, Prabhakar, a wonderful painter, and I would travel 25 kilometres one way on our days off to visit the Lalit Kala Akademi Library to explore unaffordable and expensive art books. We use to read those art books like there is no tomorrow, for seven or eight hours with a short break for a sumptuous lunch at Kaiserbagh.

Libraries have had such a profound impact on me that following my premature retirement from the Services, I wanted to try my hand at entrepreneurship by buying into a branded lending library franchise.

As a precursor, I even pursued a degree in library science, though it remained unfinished as life got in the way. Yet, to this day, I preserve that divine feeling towards libraries and the scholarly silence they so beautifully disseminate.

title: Don't stop at questioning things, have courage to find solutions: PM at IIT convocation
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
Days after a massive youth protest forced the resignation of the Union Education Minister, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said on Saturday (August 8, 2026) that “the youth should question things that are accepted without a thought, but don’t just stop at questioning; have the courage to also find their solutions.”

He was addressing new graduates at IIT-Delhi’s 57th convocation ceremony. Their degrees, he said, represent much more than academic success, serving also as a mandate to contribute to the nation.

Since mid-July, Mr. Modi has increased his outreach to youth, posting reels directly addressing them as ‘friends’ even as student protests continue in various parts of the country, seeking education reforms, particularly regarding paper leaks in competition examinations.

Also Read | PM Modi has time to meet traitors but not protesting youth: Uddhav Thackeray

Ahead of the convocation, police and paramilitary forces deployed multi-layered security, including barricades and temporary metal detectors, as well as surveillance measures. There was a ban on carrying mobile phones, bags, umbrellas, and water bottles inside the main building to prevent any possibility of disruption. The surrounding airspace was heavily monitored, restricting the use of remote-operated or unmanned aerial objects.

Problem-solving capabilities

Addressing the rapidly shifting geopolitical and strategic global landscape, the Prime Minister identified the relentless speed of technological advancement as the primary catalyst for these massive global transformations. He framed this era of rapid change as a dual landscape of unprecedented challenges and vast new opportunities. “The one who continuously learns is the one who will win,” Mr. Modi said.

During the ceremony, degrees were conferred on over 3,000 graduating students, including 587 Ph.D. scholars. Mr. Modi presented honours to students, including the President’s Gold Medal, Director’s Gold Medal, Shankar Dayal Sharma Gold Medal, and Perfect Ten Gold Medals to meritorious students. He also remotely inaugurated Param Pragya, an AI-powered high-performance supercomputing facility established at IIT-Delhi’s Sonipat campus.

The Prime Minister noted that an IIT qualification goes far beyond a high CGPA or a lucrative placement offer, acting instead as a definitive global certification of advanced problem-solving capabilities. “Your degree tells the entire world that you know exactly how to solve highly difficult problems,” he noted. 

Positive pitch

He then painted a glowing picture of some of the fields in which the graduates may seek employment or research opportunities. Highlighting the growth of the space sector following strategic government reforms, Mr. Modi lauded young engineers who are now actively designing and launching their own rockets, a feat previously restricted to a handful of nations. “Today, that same space sector has become a sky of new opportunities for thousands of our youths,” he said. 

Pointing to the rapid domestic advancement in semiconductor manufacturing, Mr. Modi noted that initial production units are already operational and driving immense national confidence. “Somewhere, a youth is proudly saying with full self-confidence: ‘First in my bloodline to make a chip in India’,” he said.

Showcasing the transformative impact of the drone sector, the Prime Minister said that young innovators are revolutionising fields ranging from agriculture and medical delivery to national defence. He added that unicorns, digital payments, and the FinTech boom, have provided unprecedented entrepreneurial platforms for millions. “All these revolutions have given millions of youths of the country an incredible opportunity to do something completely new for the first time,” he said. 

Research targets

Mr. Modi highlighted critical emerging sectors such as Artificial Intelligence, data centres, critical minerals, deep sea exploration, quantum computing, and energy security. “Many such cutting-edge fields are eagerly waiting for your immense talent, your bold innovation, and your strong leadership,” he said. 

Warning the graduates against the toxic distractions of the social media era, the Prime Minister urged them to completely avoid comparing their salaries, placements, or startup milestones with their peers. He counselled them to prioritise their mental and physical well-being while focusing strictly on self-improvement. ‘’Remember, life is absolutely not a leader-board; your real race is not with anyone else, it is with yourself,” he affirmed.

Emphasising a massive national pivot toward advanced research, Mr. Modi said that the Prime Minister’s Research Fellowship and the establishment of the Anusandhan National Research Foundation, are backed by a funding target of up to ₹1 lakh crore. “Today, the country desperately needs new research, and our administrative focus is equally and firmly on research,” he stated.

title: Eyeing citizen-centric governance and transparency, U.P. pushes digital application to track rural water projects
author: Mayank Kumar
content_html:
Aiming to bridge the gap between citizens and administration through digital platforms, the Uttar Pradesh government on Saturday emphasised that it is making robust efforts to digitally monitor rural water supply projects in real time. The government pointed out to the success of the Jal Sarthi application, which was launched in May 2026, and is supposedly being used by millions of citizens.

“Citizens can access village-level details of drinking water schemes, household tap connections, infrastructure status and implementation progress through an easy-to-use interface. Within days of its launch, more than 1.2 lakh people have downloaded the application. We are eyeing over five million downloads,” Anurag Srivastava, Additional Chief Secretary of the Namami Gange and Rural Water Supply Department, told The Hindu.

“Developed by the Uttar Pradesh Jal Nigam (Rural) and the State Water and Sanitation Mission, it brings together information relating to the Jal Jeevan Mission on a single digital platform,” he added.

Managing Director of Uttar Pradesh Jal Nigam (Rural) Raj Shekhar stressed on transparency. “Traditionally, information about government infrastructure projects remained confined to departmental records. Jal Sarathi changes that by allowing any resident to check the status of water supply schemes in their own village. For rural households, this reduces uncertainty and improves confidence in public infrastructure programmes,” said Mr. Shekhar, a 2004-batch Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officer.

Robust monitoring

Mr. Shekhar emphasised on robust monitoring. “Large-scale infrastructure programmes require robust monitoring mechanisms to ensure timely execution and quality outcomes. Digital platforms such as Jal Sarathi complement physical infrastructure by introducing real-time monitoring, geo-tagged assets and transparent reporting. Officials, engineers, gram panchayat representatives and citizens can all access the same information, reducing information asymmetry and strengthening accountability. Its unique features are attracting more users, as it’s bilingual (Hindi and English), it has easy search and selection module for public convenience and it has data at three strata : State level , district level and village wise,” said Mr. Shekhar.

The Managing Director added that the Government of India has also appreciated the feature and contents of the app on many instances. The application enables administrators to identify implementation bottlenecks, priorities interventions and improve service delivery. “As governance increasingly becomes data-driven, digital public platforms are emerging as essential tools for improving efficiency and accountability,” the officer said.

title: Kalaburagi Rangayana’s repertory to stage Shantarasa’s novel-based play ‘Sannagowdasani’
author: The Hindu Bureau
content_html:
The play ‘Sannagowdasani’, based on the acclaimed novel of the same name by renowned writer Nadoja Shantarasa, will be staged by the repertory artists of Rangayana, Kalaburagi, on August 10 at 6 p.m. and 11 at the Dr. S.M. Pandit Rangamandir in Kalaburagi.

Announcing this at a press conference at Rangayana here on Saturday, Rangayana director Sujatha Jangamshetty said the production was being organised jointly by the Department of Kannada and Culture and Rangayana, Kalaburagi.

As per the information provided by Ms. Jangamshetty, Karnataka Information Commission Chairman B. Venkata Singh will inaugurate the performances.

Joint Director of the Department of Kannada and Culture Basavaraj Hugar, Rangayana Administrative Officer Sidram Sindhe, Bagalkot Rangasamaja member Mahantesh M. Gajendragad and Kannada Prabha reporter Sheshmurthy Avadhani will be the chief guests. Playwright-adaptor Mahantesh Navalkal and director Praveen Reddy Gunjannahalli will also be present.

Writer Mahantesh Navalkal has adapted Shantarasa’s novel for the stage, while Praveen Reddy Gunjannahalli of Raichur has directed the play. Music has been composed by Raghav Kammar of Dharwad. The stage songs of Sannagowdasani and Shantarasa’s ghazals have been rendered by Raghav Kammar and his team. Rajkumar S.K. has handled the stage design and props, while Srinivas Doranahalli is in charge of lighting and has also served as co-director.

Ms. Jangamshetty said Shantarasa’s works offered a deep portrayal of rural life in the Hyderabad-Karnataka region. Sannagowdasani, while apparently narrating the story of Mehboob Jan, presents the social, political, economic and religious dimensions of village life, she said.

“The novel portrays the rivalry among village heads who stake everything for a woman, the cruelty that emerges when one loses the contest and the petty politics that disturb the lives of innocent villagers,” she said.

She said the novel presented a diverse range of characters and offered an authentic portrayal of the virtues and weaknesses of human nature. “Culture is not merely the beautiful face of life. It encompasses good and evil, truth and falsehood, social weaknesses and the complete way of life of people,” she said adding that Shantarasa’s ghazals were also incorporated into the production as a tribute to the writer.

Rangayana Administrative Officer Sidram Sindhe said Rangayana, Kalaburagi, had been established with the objective of sustaining theatre activities in the Hyderabad-Karnataka region and developing a theatre movement rooted in the region’s cultural context.

“Unlike other forms of media, theatre is a distinct and living medium. It is a matter of satisfaction that theatre is flourishing in Kalaburagi,” he said.

Following the press conference on Saturday, veteran playwright Shankarayya Ghanti released the poster of the play. A special performance of Sannagowdasani was subsequently staged for journalists.
